lead: Today's readings are about how God works: not through what the world counts as strong and impressive, but through what looks small and weak. Paul preaches “Christ crucified”, which seems foolish, yet is “the power of God and the wisdom of God”. Jesus compares the kingdom to a tiny mustard seed and to a little yeast hidden in a great mass of flour. The key words are the cross and small beginnings.

set: Paul wrote 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, probably around AD 54–55, to a young Church he had founded a few years earlier. Corinth was a rich, proud port city, and the community was splitting into groups that boasted of their favourite teachers: “I belong to Paul”, “I belong to Apollos” (1:12). Some were attracted by clever speech and philosophy.
Paul answers by going to the root: the Gospel is not a human philosophy to be admired but the message of a crucified Messiah. He quotes Isaiah 29:14 from the Greek Old Testament.
str: v. 18: the message of the cross: foolishness to some, the power of God to others.
vv. 19–21: God overturns the wisdom of the world (Isaiah 29:14).
vv. 22–24: signs, wisdom, and Christ crucified.
v. 25: the foolishness and weakness of God.
kw: Literally “the word of the cross”. Crucifixion was the most shameful death in the Roman world, kept for slaves and rebels. To preach a crucified man as Lord sounded absurd.
The word is related to our “moron”. Paul uses the very insult that was thrown at Christians and turns it around.
A trap or an obstacle that makes one trip. A crucified Messiah seemed to contradict what many expected of God's anointed one.
vv: For the message about the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.
Paul does not say “the message about wisdom” or “the message about miracles”. The power of God is found in the cross. The verbs are in the present: salvation is a road on which we are travelling.
but we proclaim Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles,

Paul, himself a Jew, describes the two great reactions he met in his preaching. He is not condemning a people; in the next verse he says that the called, “both Jews and Greeks”, find in Christ the power and wisdom of God.
For God’s foolishness is wiser than human wisdom, and God’s weakness is stronger than human strength.
A bold paradox. God has no foolishness or weakness in himself; Paul means what looks foolish and weak to us, above all the cross.
ch: The Catechism quotes these verses when it speaks of God's almighty power: it is shown most mysteriously in the voluntary humiliation and the Resurrection of his Son, so that Christ crucified is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (CCC 272). The Church does not hide the cross; she places it above the altar and signs every Christian with it.

r.h: The mustard seed and the yeast
set: Luke places these two short parables right after Jesus heals a woman who had been bent over for eighteen years, on a sabbath in a synagogue (13:10–17). The leader of the synagogue was indignant, but “the entire crowd was rejoicing” (13:17). Luke then writes, “He said therefore”: the kingdom is already at work in such small signs. Matthew gives the same two parables together (Matthew 13:31–33).
str: vv. 18–19: the mustard seed that grows into a tree where birds nest.
vv. 20–21: the yeast that leavens three measures of flour.
kw: The black mustard of Palestine has a tiny seed, proverbial for smallness, yet it can grow into a large shrub, as tall as a man or more.
Usually an image of corruption in the Bible (Luke 12:1; 1 Corinthians 5:6–8). Here Jesus surprises his hearers by using it for the kingdom.
A very large quantity of flour, enough to make bread for a great crowd. Sarah used the same amount when she baked for the three visitors at Mamre (Genesis 18:6).
vv: What is the kingdom of God like? And to what should I compare it?
Jesus looks for images from everyday life. The kingdom cannot be defined in one sentence; it is shown in pictures that set us thinking.
it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the air made nests in its branches.
The words echo Ezekiel 17:23 and Daniel 4, where a great tree shelters every kind of bird, a picture of a kingdom that gives shelter to the nations. The small seed becomes a home for many.
It is like yeast that a woman took and mixed in with three measures of flour until all of it was leavened.
The Greek verb translated “mixed in” means literally “hid”. The yeast works unseen, from within, until the whole is changed.
ch: The Second Vatican Council teaches that the Church is on earth “the initial budding forth” of the kingdom, and that while she slowly grows she longs for the completed kingdom (Lumen Gentium 5). St Ambrose, in his commentary on Luke, sees Christ himself in the mustard seed, small and despised, buried in the earth, and rising to give shelter to all (in substance). The parables give courage to small parishes, to families and to all who think their faithfulness makes no difference.

qa: If the Church is the beginning of the kingdom, why does she look so weak and small in many places?

Because God's way is the way of the mustard seed and the yeast. The kingdom grows hidden, from within, often through what seems insignificant: a family praying, a teacher's patience, a sick person offering suffering. Its growth is God's work, not a matter of numbers. Paul says the same in today's Epistle: God's weakness is stronger than human strength.
study: Where in my life have I been tempted to trust in what looks impressive rather than in the cross?
What small seed of faith or kindness can I sow today, trusting God to make it grow?
